content: Data from mainstream programs can be systematically collected and recorded across service providers. When this is done, these data can be incorporated into relevant indicators. To accurately determine the number of individuals who received an intervention during a specific time period, it is critical to avoid double-counting individuals who may have accessed the intervention multiple times within that timeframe. Unique identifier codes can be used in data collection systems to track individual clients and ensure that multiple visits by the same person are noted. However, it is essential that such systems maintain the anonymity and confidentiality of clients. Alternatively, the recall last contact method can be employed, where individuals are asked if it is their first time using the service during the reporting period. National-level coverage estimates can be more precise if the same unique identifier coding system is used across different service providers. However, due to technical challenges, it is often difficult to obtain a total count of individuals from key populations who received an intervention (numerator). This makes it challenging to estimate coverage levels relative to the need or the size of the key population (denominator). The only indicators included in this document that attempt to measure coverage in this way are those related to comprehensive condom programming. These indicators are included because data on the number of condoms distributed by key population-focused services relative to the size of the key population are often available and can serve as a useful indicator of the overall reach of these services at the national level. For example, the percentage of the total key population provided with condoms and compatible lubricant by key population-focused programs during a specified reporting period can be calculated as: (Number of people provided with condoms during the reporting period / Estimated key population size) × 100. Similarly, the total number of condoms distributed to people from key populations during the reporting period can be calculated as: (Number of condoms provided by key population-focused programs during the reporting period / Estimated key population size). Indicators that assess intervention coverage using program data require an estimate of the size of the key population in question. It is important to clearly define the population for which a size estimate is being derived. For example, if the coverage of a needle and syringe program is being estimated, the population definition should focus on people who currently inject drugs rather than those who have injected at any point in their lifetime. Determining the size of key populations can be challenging, as general population surveys, such as household surveys, may significantly underestimate the prevalence of some key populations due to stigma or reluctance to disclose sensitive behaviors or identities. Indirect estimation methods, such as multiplier and benchmark calculations using existing data sources or capture-recapture methods, are highly useful. When using information from multiple sources to estimate population size, confidentiality must always be maintained. When interpreting indicators calculated using population size estimates, it is important to consider the limitations of the estimation method and any systematic biases that may lead to overor underestimation. These limitations should also be reported when presenting results. For coverage indicators in prison and other closed settings, the number of detained individuals must be estimated. High turnover rates among detainees and the need for further disaggregation by key population may complicate this process. For example, coverage indicators for needle and syringe programs (NSP) and opioid substitution therapy (OST) require estimates of the number of detained individuals who inject drugs or are opioid-dependent. It is recommended that national expert group meetings be held regularly to evaluate available data and reach consensus on the estimates or range of estimates to be used. These meetings should involve researchers, key government personnel, NGOs, and organizations representing key populations. Where recent, high-quality estimates are unavailable, countries should make efforts to acquire such estimates. Technical and financial resources are required for these estimation activities, and external donor assistance can be sought if resource constraints exist. The Global Fund encourages countries to include population size estimation activities in funding applications and ongoing grants as part of monitoring and evaluation system strengthening. Similarly, PEPFAR supports operational research and the strengthening of monitoring and evaluation systems. If an appropriate population size estimate is not available for use as the denominator for any indicator, it is still useful and important to record and report the numerator. Numerators alone can provide valuable, albeit limited, insights into the extent of program delivery and can be particularly useful for monitoring progress over time. Intervention coverage can also be estimated through surveys of key populations. These surveys are especially important when programmatic data disaggregated by key population group are unavailable. Many indicators related to key populations in the Global AIDS Response Progress Report (GARPR) rely on this survey methodology. Surveys can capture information on risk behaviors and detailed service utilization history. However, the reliability of survey findings depends on how representative the survey sample is of the broader key population. For example, if a sample is recruited only at service sites or through peer educators, it may be biased toward individuals already in contact with services, potentially overestimating coverage levels. Indicators using survey data to measure coverage typically follow this formula: Percentage of key population who answer yes to the question: In the last [X months], have you received [NAME OF INTERVENTION]? The time period should be relevant to the intervention and context. For interventions that should be provided more frequently than once a year, shorter timeframes (e.g., one, three, or six months) are more appropriate. The quality of an intervention significantly impacts its accessibility, coverage, and effectiveness. Quality encompasses the scope, completeness, effectiveness, efficiency, safety, and acceptability of the intervention. It can be assessed through program policy reviews, key population surveys, and programmatic or administrative data. A checklist can be used to evaluate whether programs or services meet the needs of key populations and adhere to sensitivity standards. Client satisfaction surveys are also an important component of assessing intervention quality, capturing clients' perceptions of accessibility and appropriateness. Finally, health worker training is critical to ensuring that services are delivered effectively and sensitively. Workers should receive training on the specific health and welfare needs of key populations, such as men who have sex with men, people in prisons, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and transgender individuals. Monitoring the percentage of staff who have received such training is a useful indicator of program quality.
